title: The changed word
hookLine: his son Ram Rai alters a word of Nanak's hymn to please the court, and the Guru refuses to see him again

lines: THE MOST POWERFUL PERSON IN THE ROOM.
cards: You're in a meeting with the most powerful person you've ever met. They quote something your grandmother used to say, and ask what it means. The honest answer might annoy them; you can see it in their face.
So you shade it. Just one word, just enough to keep the room happy. It even has a polite name: being diplomatic.
Now change two things. The thing you shaded wasn't your grandmother's saying. It was scripture.
And the powerful person was the emperor. Today, the gentle seventh Guru draws the hardest line of his life, against his own son, over a single word.

teach.b: By 1661 there was a new emperor, Aurangzeb, who had fought his way to the throne, and he summoned Guru Har Rai to Delhi. The Guru didn't go; he sent his elder son, Ram Rai, a bright young man, to answer for the community.
At court, tradition says, Ram Rai impressed everyone. Then came a hard question.

teach.h: A LINE ABOUT CLAY AND THE POTTER.
teach.b: Someone pointed to a line in Guru Nanak's long hymn, Asa di Var. In plain words, it says the clay of a Muslim's grave ends up in the potter's hands, kneaded into pots and bricks.
It's a reflection on death: however a body is laid to rest, it becomes earth. The court heard it as an insult to Muslims.
Ram Rai, wanting to please, said it had been copied wrong, and changed the word Muslim to a word meaning a faithless person. It worked. The court was satisfied.
When the news reached Kiratpur, the gentle Guru, the one who sent medicine even to the emperor's son, was unmoved.

teach.h: THE GURU NEVER SEES HIM AGAIN.
teach.b: Tradition says he declared that Ram Rai had turned his back on the Guru's word, and he never saw his son again. He passed over him and chose his younger son, Har Krishan, as Guru. Why so hard, from so soft a man?
Because for Sikhs, the Gurus' word is not anyone's to trade, not even a Guru's son's.
Gentleness with people and firmness about the word live in the same man: he would heal an emperor's son, but he would not let one word be edited to please a throne.

how: Sikhs hold that the words of the Guru Granth Sahib must never be altered; the story of Ram Rai is told as the example of what happens when the word is changed to please power.

o: a court scholar who translated Guru Nanak's hymns
the Guru's son who changed scripture to please a court
a Mughal noble who spoke up for the Guru at court

games.q: you're Ram Rai at the emperor's court. a line of Guru Nanak's has offended the room. what do you do?
o: explain what the line really means.
say it was copied wrong, and change one word.
games.why: Ram Rai changed the word to please the court. it worked there, but his father never saw him again.

practice: Bring to mind a promise you've made that's still open: to yourself, a friend, a child, or God if you pray.

A small one is fine, like I'll call, I'll come, I'll stop, and notice any way you've been quietly rewording it, as in: I said I'd call, but a text counts. Then let the original words stand, as they were said.

wordCard.voice: Ram Rai. Guru Har Rai's elder son, who altered one word of Guru Nanak's hymn to please the emperor's court, and whom his father never saw again.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi: Asa di Var, Guru Nanak's long hymn in raga Asa, traditionally sung in the early morning.

carryVoice: Your line: don't change the word. Tomorrow, the younger son he chose instead. That's day seventy-one.
